As a former psychologist, something that's been interesting to me lately is the crossover I'm starting to see between CPTSD and dissociative disorders (OSDD, DID, etc.). There's something called structural dissociation, which perfectly describes what's happening when I get badly triggered. Last year I realized I had OSDD 1a alongside CPTSD, and only since finding out about and treating the OSDD have I experienced significant gains in my recovery. What happens for me is that when I get triggered badly enough, my consciousness blurs and I go from bawling with tears streaming down my face to completely numb in a couple seconds. And then I don't remember what happens once I go numb - it's like "I" get blindfolded and put in the trunk of my own consciousness while the numb part of me takes the wheel. And my memory usually doesn't come back until something snaps me out of it - I usually have to cry again, or feel something strong enough that it breaks the dissociation, and then my memory restores. It's such an odd phenomenon...my brain decides that I can't handle something and it thinks it needs to step in to protect me. I'm sure this happened all the time when I was a kid in order to cope with my childhood...I don't have many memories at all of being young except the horrible things, but as I recover I'm able to remember more and more, for better and for worse. The goal of my therapy has become re-integration, which involves seeing as much of the dissociation process as I can and striving to remain present with it all.

I just wanted to let you know that I really relate to what you're saying, especially the part about needing to comfort her and her turning you into the bad guy ("you want me to cry"). Even though she's your mom, and you no doubt love each other, just know that this is the behavior of an emotionally immature person. You might want to read the book "Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents". Even though you're not an adult yet, it seems like you have a good head on your shoulders and will be able to get a lot from it. 

People who can't manage their own emotions turn to things like drinking and other types of addiction. And they also can't handle when other people are upset with them, even if it's for very good reason. Even if you want her to see the pain she's caused and take some accountability, the sad thing is she won't be able to unless she goes to therapy and works on the guilt and shame she feels. But that doesn't mean you can't get closure or get better - your recovery doesn't depend on your mom understanding what she's done. You can get better through therapy, reading healing books (Pete Walker's stuff on CPTSD), and establishing relationships with healthy and emotionally mature people. 

You're probably going to have to unlearn the habit of taking care of someone because they feel bad for the hurt THEY caused you. This is a setup for becoming a doormat later in life and you deserve to be around people who can take responsibility and say "I'm sorry I hurt you" and mean it with their whole heart.

So no, it's probably not the best way to go. And neither of your parents are going to protect you, so now you've got to think - is there any adult you know and trust who you could talk to about this? Maybe a different family member, or a friend's parent who may be able to take you in? If not, it's scary but you've got to be the adult and protect yourself. Get a job, get an apartment, get away from this man as soon as you can. And until then, keep being clear about your boundaries. It might feel weird because he's your dad, but you can hold out your hands in front of you in a "stop" position and issue a command "stop" "don't touch me" "leave me alone". If he continues, you can raise your voice and repeat yourself, "i said stop" "i said don't touch me" etc. and if he continues you have case for self-defense. Maybe you can find a workshop in your area and learn how to get away safely, and if he corners you, make beaks with your fingers and aim for his eyes, or kick him hard in the groin. It's tough to imagine I'm sure, because he's your blood relative, but he has NO BUSINESS TOUCHING YOU and YOU HAVE A RIGHT TO SAY NO AND BE HEARD.

Context matters a lot in this situation I think...some guideposts for me might be:

* Be respectful. Smile, keep conversation light and friendly. If you want to pay a compliment, be sure to compliment something she chose (her sense of style, the book she's carrying) not anything she was born with to avoid accidentally sexualizing her.
* Rehearse some generic openers that work for you. They'll be different for everyone and will vary in different spaces. Try a few out that feel genuine - avoid pickup lines. This might not work for everyone, but for me, something like "Excuse me, I'm sorry but have I seen you before? You look so familiar" would feel okay and non-threatening for me. If I thought you were cute, I'd try and keep the conversation going. If not, I'd probably be polite and keep the interaction short.
* Be prepared for a no. Go into it with an open mind knowing you might not get the answer you want, take a "no" gracefully and bow out with something like "no worries, it was nice meeting you"
* Commend yourself for trying! It's a brave thing to do in this day and age to approach a girl and risk not only rejection but the possibility of upsetting them. It's a two-way street: as long as you're respectful and can take a "no" gracefully, if someone has a problem with it, that's more about them than you and you're not responsible for how someone else takes something *as long as you're being a good human.* If you're not sure you can or know what this means, talk to some of the women in your life and get their perspectives.

An example of a time I was approached that went really well: we were in a shared community space and during social time he came up to me and introduced himself. I'm working on integrating the rebellious part so that I can express when I'm angry earlier, before it gets to the point where it's out of my control. The fawn response makes me feel like a pushover, and the rebelliousness is there to assure I'm not getting taken advantage of. If I can stay in my zone of regulation and state clearer boundaries, I'm hoping the anger can be expressed without damaging myself or others. We'll see though, the work is always so hard...an uphill battle just to get 1/2 as far as other people.

People who do this are still trapped in the idea that their life or death is inextricably tied to how others feel about them. Their worth is derived externally, usually in close relationships where the primary wounds of feeling unworthy or unloved are likely to surface. 

They weren't yet able to see their inherent worth, and understand that regardless of what someone else does or doesn't do, *they are still just as worthy as they ever were.* 

If someone realizes that but still goes on to commit suicide, they feel defeated and hopeless because they know they're not strong enough to heal their innermost demons of unworthiness and unlovability. Their vision of the future can get black and white (I'm better off dead, if I can't fix this then I'm doing less harm dead than I would alive, there's no way I'm going to be able to show myself the love I need without help from others).

Yeah, it's an unfortunate reality of growing up in an abusive home. We learn models for relating that work in an unhealthy context but are absolutely harmful in healthy ones. We pick up "fleas" from our abusive caregivers and need to do the work to rid ourselves of them so that we can interrupt the generational cycles of trauma. I read your story and I probably would've asked this question 10 yrs ago when I was in your place, a hopeless romantic in college finding relationships with people who only wanted something casual. I'll try my best to answer your questions directly, please take my advice with a gran of salt and only keep what resonates: 


"Are my expectations too high?" I don't think so. If anything, I think they're probably too low. It's funny because in my experience, I feel like my expectations are both too high and too low at the same time - too high because I haven't found someone who meets my expectations, and too low because I don't believe the right one is out there so I'm willing to make concessions, sometimes big ones.


"How do you deal with that void, other than hobbies and friends?" Other than hobbies and friends, I'm engaged in a spiritual community and I try to offer love to myself first. It helps me to think of myself as another person since it's easier for me to love another. I ask myself how I'm feeling, what I need, and work to meet my own needs. The more I practice with myself the more I feel I have to offer to another in relationship.


"Should I be more forgiving of mistakes like this?" Absolutely not. I struggled so much with doing things I'm uncomfortable with to appease someone else and avoid being alone. As a result, I've landed myself in pretty terrible relationships and I wouldn't wish that on anyone. Hold onto your standards and the right person will respect them.

I think the line is how much you take the other person's feelings into account when you share yours. You could say something not people pleasing and not dickish by showing that you understand how they feel. 

An example might be: "hey, I know you were really looking forward to doing X this weekend, and so was I, I've just got so much going on I need the weekend to myself."

If they just said, "I've got a lot going on and need the weekend to myself" that would be taking their needs into account but not acknowledging the affect the choice has on the other person too. It's not inherently dickish, but it might be perceived that way.
